lessonTitle: Inspection, Palpation and Percussion of the Abdomen

blocks.text: A 24-year-old student describes a vague ache around her umbilicus that has migrated overnight to the lower right side of her abdomen. When you press gently there, she tightens her abdominal wall and winces. Knowing which organ sits beneath each area and how to read that muscle tightening is what turns an ache into a localised clinical finding.

blocks.markdown: The abdomen is a large, soft cavity with no bony landmarks to guide you, so examiners divide it into **regions**. Naming the region where a sign appears tells you which organs lie beneath and which diagnoses to consider. The same logic guides the three hands-on phases of examination: **inspect** first, **palpate** (gently, then deeply), then **percuss**, always looking at the patient's face for signs of pain.

blocks.title: Abdominal regions
blocks.text: The **nine regions** are defined by two vertical (midclavicular) lines and two horizontal planes (subcostal above and transtubercular below). From top left to bottom right: right hypochondrium, epigastrium, left hypochondrium; right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar; right iliac fossa, hypogastrium (suprapubic), left iliac fossa. A simpler scheme uses **four quadrants** divided by horizontal and vertical lines through the umbilicus.

blocks.caption: Regions and the organs usually found beneath them (clinical teaching guide; organs vary in position)
rows: Right lobe of liver, gallbladder, right kidney (upper pole)
Stomach, spleen, left kidney (upper pole), tail of pancreas
Ascending colon, lower pole of right kidney
Small bowel loops, transverse colon, aorta
Descending colon, lower pole of left kidney
Bladder if full, uterus if enlarged, small bowel

blocks.title: Using regions to build a differential
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old man points to a tender area in the right hypochondrium after fatty meals. Name the region and list the structures that lie beneath it that could be responsible.

steps.text: Identify the region from the description: below the right costal margin and lateral to the midclavicular line is the right hypochondrium.
List the structures beneath it from the table: liver, gallbladder and the upper pole of the right kidney.
Use the history to rank them: pain after fatty meals points to the biliary system, so the gallbladder moves to the top of the list.
Plan the examination: palpate gently, then check for tenderness on deep inspiration over the gallbladder fundus.

blocks.answer: Right hypochondrium; liver, gallbladder and right kidney lie beneath, and the gallbladder is most likely given the pain after fatty meals.

blocks.markdown:
### Inspection

Stand at the foot of the couch with the patient lying flat and relaxed. Look for **distension**, scars, visible masses or pulsation, skin changes, an everted umbilicus, and movement with respiration. Then move to the patient's right side, kneel or sit so your eyes and hands are at the level of the abdomen, and keep watching the face.

### Palpation: light, then deep, and the signs of peritonism

**Light palpation** uses the flat of the fingers pressed gently into each of the nine regions, beginning away from any pain, to detect tenderness, superficial masses and muscle resistance. **Deep palpation** uses firmer pressure to detect masses and organs.

**Peritonism** (peritoneal irritation) is suggested by:

- **Guarding**: voluntary or involuntary tightening of the abdominal wall muscles when palpated.
- **Rigidity**: a board-like wall that stays tight despite relaxation; it suggests generalised peritonitis.
- **Rebound tenderness**: pain on sudden release of pressure, greater than the pain on pressing in. Many teachers prefer percussion tenderness or the cough test because rebound is itself painful.
- Pain on coughing or when the bed is jolted.

blocks.title: Guarding versus voluntary tension
blocks.text: A patient who is cold, anxious or ticklish may tighten voluntarily. True guarding is reflex and persists when the patient is distracted or breathes out. Warm hands, a clear explanation and bent knees reduce voluntary tension.

blocks.caption: Peritoneal signs compared
rows: Pressure then rapid release causes pain
Gentle tap over the area hurts
Peritoneal inflammation, less painful than rebound

blocks.markdown:
### Organs and fluid

**Liver.** Start in the right iliac fossa and move your hand up toward the right costal margin in time with the patient's breathing, asking for a deep breath in. A liver edge felt below the costal margin may be enlarged (**hepatomegaly**) or pushed down, for example by hyperinflated lungs. Percuss the upper border (normally around the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line) to check whether the liver is truly enlarged.

**Spleen.** Start in the right iliac fossa and move diagonally toward the left costal margin. The spleen must enlarge about two to three times before it becomes palpable. An enlarged spleen has a **notch**, moves down on inspiration, cannot be "got above" and enlarges toward the right iliac fossa.

**Ascites.** Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity causes flank bulging and dullness. Test with **shifting dullness**: percuss from the midline toward the flank until the note turns dull, keep the finger there, roll the patient away and re-percuss after about 30 seconds; if the note becomes resonant, free fluid has shifted.

blocks.title: Performing shifting dullness
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old man with chronic liver disease has a protuberant abdomen. Describe the steps for shifting dullness and interpret a note that is dull in the left flank when supine but resonant when he lies on his right side.

steps.text: With the patient supine, percuss from the umbilicus (resonant, gas-filled bowel) outward toward the left flank until the note becomes dull. Leave the finger in place.
Roll the patient onto the right side so the dull flank is uppermost, and wait about 30 seconds for fluid to settle by gravity.
Percuss again at the same spot. If it is now resonant, the fluid has moved to the dependent side and bowel has floated up to replace it.
Interpret: dullness that shifts with posture indicates free peritoneal fluid, so ascites is likely.

blocks.answer: Dullness that becomes resonant on turning means the dullness was moving fluid: free ascites.

items: Always inspect before palpating, and watch the patient's face throughout.
Palpate gently first and begin away from the painful area.
Document the region, the tenderness, and whether guarding is voluntary or reflex.
Describe any mass by site, size, shape, surface, edge, consistency, tenderness, pulsatility and mobility with respiration.
Percuss the liver borders and test for shifting dullness when ascites is suspected.

blocks.title: Do not delay for a rigid abdomen
blocks.text: A rigid, silent abdomen with a very unwell patient suggests generalised peritonitis. Stop the examination, assess the vital signs and escalate to a senior colleague immediately.

points: The abdomen is divided into nine regions (or four quadrants) so that signs can be related to underlying organs.
Palpate gently first, then deeply; guarding, rigidity and rebound or percussion tenderness are signs of peritonism.
Palpate the liver and spleen from the right iliac fossa upward in time with breathing; percuss the liver border to confirm enlargement.
Test for ascites with shifting dullness; dullness that moves with posture indicates free fluid.

questions.stem: In the nine-region scheme, the region directly below the umbilical region and in the midline is called the:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the midline lower region, also called suprapubic.
distractorRationale.b: The epigastrium lies above the umbilical region.
distractorRationale.c: Lumbar regions are lateral, beside the umbilical region.
distractorRationale.d: The hypochondria are the upper lateral regions.

questions.explanation: The central column of the nine regions runs epigastrium, umbilical, hypogastrium from above downward. The hypogastrium (suprapubic region) lies below the umbilical region.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has tenderness localised to the left iliac fossa. Which structure normally lies beneath this region?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the sigmoid and descending colon lie in the left iliac fossa.
distractorRationale.b: The caecum is in the right iliac fossa.
distractorRationale.c: The gallbladder is in the right hypochondrium.
distractorRationale.d: The spleen is in the left hypochondrium.

questions.explanation: Colon anatomy maps to regions: caecum and appendix in the right iliac fossa, sigmoid in the left. Knowing the region therefore narrows the differential for the source of pain.

questions.stem: A man with severe abdominal pain has a board-like abdominal wall that stays tense whether he breathes in or out and during distraction. This finding is best described as:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: persistent board-like tension indicates rigidity of the abdominal wall.
distractorRationale.b: Voluntary guarding relaxes with distraction and expiration.
distractorRationale.c: Ballotment refers to the sensation of a kidney or fluid mass moving on palpation.
distractorRationale.d: A cough impulse is a hernia sign.

questions.explanation: Rigidity is constant, involuntary muscle spasm and suggests generalised peritonitis. Voluntary guarding eases when the patient relaxes or is distracted.

questions.stem: When palpating the abdomen of a patient who reports pain in the right iliac fossa, where should you begin?

options.text: Away from the painful area, in the opposite region
Directly over the painful area, with deep pressure
In the right iliac fossa with sudden release
At the xiphisternum with the patient sitting

questions.correctOptionText: Away from the painful area, in the opposite region

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beginning away from pain builds trust and avoids false guarding.
distractorRationale.b: Deep pressure first causes pain and voluntary guarding.
distractorRationale.c: Sudden release is not an opening manoeuvre.
distractorRationale.d: Standard palpation is done with the patient supine.

questions.explanation: Starting away from the painful region lets the patient relax and gives a baseline. Examining the painful area last prevents early guarding that masks other findings.

questions.stem: You feel a mass in the left hypochondrium that descends on inspiration, has a palpable notch on its medial edge and has no palpable upper border (you cannot get above it). The most likely organ is:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: notch, downward movement on inspiration and no upper border are the classic splenic features.
distractorRationale.b: A kidney is ballotable, has no notch and you can usually get above it.
distractorRationale.c: The colon does not move with respiration in this way.
distractorRationale.d: The stomach is not palpable as a notched mass.

questions.explanation: The enlarged spleen expands from beneath the left costal margin toward the right iliac fossa, so you cannot palpate above it, and it moves with the diaphragm. A kidney, in contrast, is bimanually palpable and ballotable.

questions.stem: True or false: shifting dullness in which the percussion note over the flank changes from dull to resonant when the patient is rolled onto the opposite side suggests free peritoneal fluid.
questions.explanation: Free fluid moves to the dependent flank when the patient rolls, while gas-filled bowel floats to the top. The resulting change in note from dull to resonant at the same site is the sign of ascites.

questions.stem: Which statement about palpating for hepatomegaly is correct?

options.text: Start in the right iliac fossa and move upward in time with respiration, then percuss the upper border to confirm a true enlargement
Start at the costal margin and move down so as not to miss a low edge
A palpable liver edge always means the liver is enlarged
The upper border is percussed in the midline over the epigastrium

questions.correctOptionText: Start in the right iliac fossa and move upward in time with respiration, then percuss the upper border to confirm a true enlargement

distractorRationale.a: Correct: starting low avoids missing a massively enlarged liver and percussion confirms the size.
distractorRationale.b: Starting at the costal margin can miss a liver that reaches the pelvis.
distractorRationale.c: A liver pushed down by hyperinflated lungs may be palpable without being enlarged.
distractorRationale.d: The upper border is percussed in the midclavicular line, not the midline.

questions.explanation: Beginning in the right iliac fossa guarantees you will not step over a very large liver. Because a normal liver may be pushed down by emphysema, percussion of the upper border distinguishes true hepatomegaly from displacement.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has severe lower abdominal pain. List the findings on palpation and percussion that would indicate peritonism, and explain how you would distinguish true guarding from voluntary tensing.
markingGuide: Percussion tenderness or pain on coughing
Voluntary tensing eases with distraction, relaxation and expiration
Warm hands, explanation, flexed knees and starting away from the pain reduce voluntary tension
questions.explanation: Peritonism reflects irritation of the parietal peritoneum, which produces reflex muscle contraction and tenderness on movement. Distinguishing reflex guarding from voluntary tensing depends on whether the tension persists when the patient is relaxed or distracted.

questions.stem: Describe how you would examine a 65-year-old man for splenomegaly and list three features that identify a palpable mass as the spleen.
markingGuide: Consent, positioning supine with knees slightly flexed
Start in the right iliac fossa and move toward the left costal margin in time with respiration
Ask the patient to breathe in deeply
Percuss over it and compare with kidney (ballotable, can get above)
questions.explanation: Starting low avoids missing a very large spleen. The notch, downward movement with respiration and absence of an upper border distinguish the spleen from the left kidney.

questions.stem: Explain how the nine abdominal regions are used in clinical examination, and give the region and underlying organ you would think of for a tender area that lies below and to the right of the umbilicus in the right iliac fossa.
markingGuide: Regions are defined by two vertical midclavicular lines and two horizontal planes
Naming the region localises the sign to underlying organs and narrows the differential
Caecum, appendix and terminal ileum named as underlying structures
Notes that organ positions vary between patients
questions.explanation: Regions provide a common language for describing where a sign is found. The right iliac fossa overlies the caecum, appendix and terminal ileum, so appendicitis would be among the leading considerations in a suitable history.
